codebook.source: MONK-2 problem (Thrun et al. 1991), PMLB 'monk2' deduplicated to the 432 input configurations; attributes a1-a6 are abstract (no real-world meaning), so statements are phrased in rule terms on the attribute values

sentences.text: This gate reads all six attributes, a4 and a5 through a small pool, and acts on 92 of 345 training cases, 3 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on (no attribute at its first value), it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without it to below 1% with it.

How much a6 = 2 instead of 1 moves the prediction depends on a1 and a3: for the typical case, it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 77% when a1 is not 1 and to about 68% when a3 = 2, but leaves it below 1% when a1 = 1 or a3 = 1.
Through it, moving a1, a3 or a6 away from its first value lowers the probability and a2 = 1 or 2 instead of 3 raises it, all below 1% for the typical case it acts on.

This ramp adds up all six attributes with fixed weights: through it, moving a1, a6, a3 or a5 away from its first value raises the predicted probability of 'yes', and giving a2 or a4 its first value lowers it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.

The model predicts 'yes' when exactly two of a1 to a6 take their first value, and otherwise not: at every count, at least 97% of the training cases get the same prediction, and the average training case with two attributes at their first value gets about 78%, against about 1% for the other counts.

lead.text: For the typical case (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1) the model gives a predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%; it combines two parts, a gate on all six attributes and a ramp that adds them up, and follows the exactly-two rule.

evidence.text: How a4 = 1 instead of 2 acts through it depends on a5: it goes one way when a5 = 4 and the other way when a5 = 1, with the typical case below 1% either way.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

parts.name: exactly_two_window
parts.original_hypothesis: Exactly-two window = descending ramp minus low-count veto. Output = sigmoid(1.383 + Ramp - 4.009 Veto - 0.888 Pool). The linear part (bias + ramp + pool readout) by number of active first-value indicators: 0 -> 18.1, 1 -> 9.2 to 13.8, 2 -> 0.49 to 5.67, 3 -> -8.0 to -2.75, 4 or more -> below -11.5; it is positive iff at most two indicators are active (upper edge of the window). The veto is at least 5.16 whenever at most one indicator is active, so -4.009 Veto <= -20.7 overrides the ramp's maximum of 18.1 (lower edge). The output is therefore above 0.5 exactly when two indicators are active, with one exception: for count two made of a2=1 and a5=1, the veto leaks 0.62, and 0.62 x 4.009 = 2.49 exceeds the ramp margin 1.56 (pre-activation -0.93), so the 4 such configurations (a1 in {2,3}, a2=1, a3=2, a4 in {2,3}, a5=1, a6=2) are scored negative. The inputs a1:2, a1:3, a2:2, a3:2, a4:3, a5:2, a5:3 have no enabled connections and zero effect; they are listed here as zero-effect entry nodes. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): accuracy 0.991, AUC 1.000. Linear part (bias + ramp - 0.888 pool) per count: 0 -> 18.11; 1 -> 9.22..13.75; 2 -> 0.49..5.67; 3 -> -7.98..-2.75; 4 -> -16.39..-11.48; 5 -> -24.48..-20.37; 6 -> -29.50. Output > 0.5 for 0% of count 0/1/3/4/5/6 rows and 97.3% of count 2 rows; the 3 misses are the a2=1,a5=1 veto leak (output 0.283). Sensitivity of the output: veto 0.213, ramp 0.053, pool 0.047, all seven unconnected inputs 0.0. Over all 432 configurations the network agrees with 'exactly two indicators' on 428 (the 4 a2=1,a5=1 count-2 configurations are the only disagreements).

parts.name: low_count_veto_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Low-count veto gate, a serial composition Veto(a1, a2, a3, a6, Pool(a4, a5)). Node 288 = ReLU(17.125 - 10.71 I1 - 7.81 I2 + 0.74 [a2=3] - 9.85 I3 - 11.82 I6 - 3.378 Pool). Through the pool, I4 alone subtracts 10.3 (12.0 when a5=4), I5 alone 8.7, both 21.5. Every active first-value indicator thus removes 7.8 to 11.8 from a bias of 17.1: the gate is on (5.16 to 17.87) for every configuration with zero or one active indicators and off for two or more, with one exception: I2 + I5 (a2=1 and a5=1) leaves 17.125 - 7.81 - 8.69 = 0.62 > 0, a small leak. So 288 detects 'at most one of the six rule indicators is active'. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample), by number of active first-value indicators: count 0 (19 rows) gate 17.13..17.87, on 100%; count 1 (70) gate 5.16..9.32, on 100%; count 2 (113) on 2.7% (3 rows, all a2=1 and a5=1, value 0.62); count >=3 (143) off 100%. Sensitivities: a6:1 1.58, a1:1 1.37, a3:1 1.31, a2:1 0.98, pool 0.90, a2:3 0.09. Over all 432 configurations the same pattern holds (on for count <=1; on at count 2 only for the 4 a2=1,a5=1 configurations).

parts.name: a4_a5_first_value_pool
parts.original_hypothesis: A4/a5 first-value pool (with an inert a4:2 sub-unit). Write I_k for 'attribute k takes its first value'. In indicator form node 389 = ReLU(-0.744 + 3.793 I4 + 3.317 I5 + 0.492 [a5=4] - 0.0006 u), where u = node 2443 = ReLU(0.997 [a4=2] - 1.281) is identically zero on the whole domain (maximum pre-activation -0.284), so the a4:2 branch is inert (and its readout weight is -0.0006 anyway). With neither a4 nor a5 at its first value the pool outputs 0 (pre-activation -0.744 or -0.252); a4=1 alone gives 3.05 (3.54 when a5=4), a5=1 alone gives 2.57, both give 6.37. The pool is therefore a rectified, near-additive count of the two rule indicators I4 and I5, which the downstream gate does not receive directly. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): node 2443 is 0 on every row; sensitivity of the pool to a4:2 is 0.0, to a4:1 0.86, a5:1 0.71, a5:4 0.10. The pool takes exactly five values on train: 0 (176 rows), 2.573 (a5=1, 62), 3.049 (a4=1, 57), 3.541 (a4=1, a5=4, 25), 6.366 (a4=1 and a5=1, 25).

parts.name: linear_count_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: Linear descending count ramp. In indicator form the direct input-to-output connections sum to 16.73 - 8.89 I1 - 8.08 I2 - 8.41 I3 - 1.66 I4 - 6.19 I5 - 8.73 I6 (exact; a6 enters through its complement a6:2 with +8.73, the same signal inverted). Every first-value indicator lowers the score by 6 to 9, except I4 (-1.66), whose shortfall is made up at the root by the pool readout (-0.888 x Pool, i.e. about -2.7 for I4 and -2.3 for I5). The ramp falls approximately linearly with the number of active rule indicators. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): sensitivities equal the absolute weights (a1:1 4.25, a2:1 3.82, a3:1 4.20, a4:1 0.77, a5:1 2.69, a6:2 4.36), as expected for a linear map. Indicator-form least squares fit over all 432 configurations is exact (residual 5.5e-14): 16.73 - 8.89 I1 - 8.08 I2 - 8.41 I3 - 1.66 I4 - 6.19 I5 - 8.73 I6.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
